questions.prompt: You have built and tested an application locally. The publish directory contains all ready-to-run files, including the entry point. ZIP deployment will use its default extraction path with build automation disabled. Which archive layout should you deploy?

options.text: Place the contents of the publish directory directly at the ZIP root.
options.explanation: ZIP deployment extracts into the app content directory. Putting the published contents at the archive root preserves the expected entry-point layout.

options.text: Place the publish directory itself at the ZIP root with the files nested inside it.
options.explanation: Including the enclosing publish directory adds a level below the app content root instead of placing the entry point at its expected location.

options.text: Place the published files inside a wwwroot directory at the ZIP root.
options.explanation: The default deployment destination is already wwwroot. This extra directory nests the application one level too deep.

options.text: Place the unbuilt source directory contents directly at the ZIP root.
options.explanation: Build automation is disabled. The archive needs the tested ready-to-run output rather than source that still requires build tasks.

questions.prompt: What happens when an administrator changes App Service app settings?

options.text: The updated settings are passed as environment variables after an app restart.
options.explanation: App Service injects app settings into the runtime environment and triggers an app restart when settings are added, removed, or edited.

options.text: The updated settings become environment variables without restarting the running app.
options.explanation: A settings edit triggers a restart; it is not merely an in-place change to the running process environment.

options.text: The updated settings are written into source configuration files before a rebuild.
options.explanation: App settings are runtime environment configuration. Saving them does not require rewriting source files and rebuilding the application.

options.text: The updated settings remain pending until the next application package deployment.
options.explanation: Saving an app-settings change triggers the restart that applies it; a separate package deployment is not required.

questions.prompt: An App Service app reads blobs using a token for its system-assigned managed identity. Token acquisition and network access succeed, but blob reads fail authorization. The identity has no blob data role, and no deny assignments or role conditions apply. Which role assignment authorizes this app to read the blobs?

options.text: Assign Storage Blob Data Reader to the app identity at the target container.
options.explanation: The app uses its managed identity for blob data requests. This role grants that principal read access to blobs in the target container.

options.text: Assign Reader to the app identity at the storage account.
options.explanation: Reader grants management-plane visibility, not the blob data permissions needed for token-authenticated reads.

options.text: Assign Website Contributor to the app identity at the web app.
options.explanation: Permission to manage the web app does not grant its identity read access to the target container data.

options.text: Assign Storage Blob Data Reader to the deployment user at the target container.
options.explanation: The request token represents the app identity, not the deployment user. Granting the user access does not authorize the app principal.

questions.prompt: A Standard App Service app has automatic backups. It writes business documents to a custom-mounted Azure Files share. Recovery must restore both the app and those documents after accidental deletion. Which protection plan covers the separately stored documents?

options.text: Keep app backups and separately protect and test restoration of the Azure Files share.
options.explanation: Custom-mounted storage is excluded from App Service backups. Separate share protection and restore procedures cover the business documents.

options.text: Keep automatic app backups and use an app restore to recover the mounted-share documents.
options.explanation: Automatic app backups exclude custom-mounted Azure storage, so their app recovery points do not contain these documents.

options.text: Replace automatic app backups with custom app backups and recover the share from their ZIP files.
options.explanation: Custom app backups retain the same custom-mounted-storage exclusion; changing app backup type does not add the external documents.

options.text: Keep app backups and restore the storage mount configuration to recover the share documents.
options.explanation: Restoring a connection or mount configuration does not restore the external share content excluded from the app backup.

questions.prompt: A production web app on a Standard App Service plan is serving users. You must demonstrate that an app backup produces a working application before replacing production content. Production must keep serving during the test. A disposable staging slot and isolated test dependencies are available. Which recovery test meets these requirements?

options.text: Restore into the staging slot and test the recovered app against the isolated dependencies.
options.explanation: App Service stops the restore target, so using the staging slot preserves the production endpoint while functional checks establish recovery evidence.

options.text: Restore over production and test it after the restore completes.
options.explanation: An in-place restore stops and overwrites the production target, violating the requirement to keep it serving during the test.

options.text: Inspect the backup status and timestamp, then approve production replacement without restoring.
options.explanation: Job metadata does not demonstrate that the recovered application starts and works with its required dependencies.

options.text: Restore into staging and check only the recovered file count before approving replacement.
options.explanation: File presence alone does not establish working application behavior or successful access to the required test dependencies.

questions.prompt: In October 2026, you design a new App Service recovery setup with Azure SQL. Which database backup approach follows current Microsoft guidance?

options.text: Use Azure SQL native backup and restore alongside app protection.
options.explanation: Microsoft recommends native database tools, and new linked SQL backup configurations were removed in April 2026.

options.text: Depend on creating a new App Service linked SQL backup configuration.
options.explanation: The documented removal schedule has already removed this option for new configurations.

options.text: Assume automatic App Service backups include the SQL database.
options.explanation: Automatic backups do not include linked databases.

options.text: Use a deployment-slot swap as the only database backup.
options.explanation: A slot swap does not create a recoverable database backup.

questions.prompt: You map www.example.com to an App Service app and want DNS to follow its default hostname rather than a fixed IP. Which routing record does Microsoft recommend?

options.text: A CNAME from www to the app default hostname.
options.explanation: CNAME maps the subdomain to the hostname.

options.text: A TXT record containing only the app IP.
options.explanation: TXT verification is not traffic routing.

options.text: An MX record targeting the app hostname.
options.explanation: MX controls mail delivery, not web traffic resolution.

options.text: An NS record delegating www to the app hostname.
options.explanation: An app hostname is not an authoritative DNS nameserver.

questions.prompt: You configure ownership verification for www.example.com. App Service displays a domain verification ID. Which TXT record in the example.com DNS zone uses that ID for this subdomain?

options.text: Name: asuid.www; value: the app domain verification ID.
options.explanation: For the www subdomain, App Service looks up asuid.www and compares its value with the app domain verification ID.

options.text: Name: asuid; value: the app domain verification ID.
options.explanation: The asuid record without the subdomain prefix is used for the apex; it is not the documented verification record for www.example.com.

options.text: Name: www; value: the app domain verification ID.
options.explanation: The subdomain ownership TXT name requires the asuid.www prefix, not simply www.

options.text: Name: asuid.www; value: the app default hostname.
options.explanation: The record name is correct but its value must be the verification ID. The default hostname belongs in the routing CNAME.

questions.prompt: A Standard App Service app has production and staging endpoints. The production default hostname works. A client resolves www.example.com to the production endpoint, and asuid.www matches its verification ID. HTTP requests using www.example.com return a platform 404. The production app has no custom-hostname entry for www.example.com. Which hostname configuration fixes that missing production mapping?

options.text: Validate and add www.example.com to the production app custom hostnames.
options.explanation: The requested Host header must be associated with the intended production app. DNS routing and ownership verification alone do not add that hostname mapping.

options.text: Validate and add example.com to the production app custom hostnames.
options.explanation: The apex and www are different hostnames; adding only example.com does not register the requested www.example.com name.

options.text: Validate and add www.example.com only to the staging slot custom hostnames.
options.explanation: That associates the name with staging, while the required destination is production. A slot mapping does not add a production mapping.

options.text: Publish another asuid.www TXT record without adding an app hostname entry.
options.explanation: The existing verification ID is already correct. Additional ownership proof does not create the missing hostname-to-app association.

questions.prompt: An App Service app must call a VM using its private IP in a same-region VNet. Which App Service networking feature provides the outbound VNet path?

options.text: Regional VNet integration
options.explanation: It routes outbound calls from the app into the integrated network.

options.text: Only a private endpoint for the web app
options.explanation: That provides inbound private access to the app.

options.text: Only an app custom-domain binding
options.explanation: A hostname binding does not create the outbound VNet path.

options.text: Only an inbound IP access restriction
options.explanation: Inbound filtering does not configure private outbound routing.

questions.prompt: A Standard App Service app has no VNet integration or private endpoint. VNet clients must reach it through a private IP, and the app must connect to a database VM private IP in the same-region VNet. Suitable separate subnets, required permissions, and database access are available. Which TWO capabilities jointly supply the inbound and outbound paths? Configure private DNS for the inbound endpoint and disable app public access as part of the design.

options.text: Create and approve an App Service private endpoint for the client-to-app path.
options.explanation: The endpoint gives VNet clients a private inbound address for the app. It supplies this half of the design, while outbound database access needs integration.

options.text: Configure regional VNet integration for the app-to-database path.
options.explanation: Integration routes outbound app calls into the VNet toward the private database VM. It supplies this half without providing private inbound app access.

options.text: Create only a private DNS A record for the app without a private endpoint.
options.explanation: DNS can resolve an address but cannot create the private endpoint network interface or the inbound service connection.

options.text: Add an inbound allow rule for VNet clients on the app integration subnet NSG.
options.explanation: Integration-subnet inbound rules do not expose the app privately. They cannot replace its private endpoint or provide the outbound integration attachment.

questions.prompt: A Standard web app uses subnet-app for regional VNet integration. You must add its inbound private endpoint without changing existing subnet delegations. All subnets below are in the same VNet and have available IP addresses. Which subnet can host the private endpoint?

options.text: subnet-private: no service delegation.
options.explanation: A nondelegated subnet with available addresses can host the private endpoint, and it is separate from the integration subnet.

options.text: subnet-app: delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms and used by this app integration.
options.explanation: The private endpoint must not share the integration subnet; a delegated subnet cannot host the private endpoint.

options.text: subnet-containers: delegated to Microsoft.ContainerInstance/containerGroups.
options.explanation: Private endpoints cannot be deployed in a subnet delegated to a service, even when addresses remain available.

options.text: subnet-other-plan: delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms for another plan integration.
options.explanation: A different integration plan does not remove this subnet delegation; it still cannot host the private endpoint.

questions.prompt: Two web apps and a staging slot run in the same Standard App Service plan. Per-app scaling is disabled. How are the worker instances used?

options.text: Both apps and the slot share the worker instances allocated to the plan.
options.explanation: With per-app scaling disabled, apps and deployment slots run on the same plan instances and share their CPU and memory.

options.text: Each app has its own worker instances, and the slot shares only its parent app instances.
options.explanation: Dedicated compute is allocated to the plan, not separately to each app; both apps share the plan workers.

options.text: Both apps share the plan workers, and the slot receives a separate worker allocation.
options.explanation: Deployment slots also use the plan workers; creating a slot does not create an independent compute allocation.

options.text: The plan divides its workers into nonoverlapping allocations for the two apps and the slot.
options.explanation: Per-app scaling is disabled, so each runs on the plan instances rather than receiving a separate partition of workers.

questions.prompt: An existing Standard App Service plan hosts a customer portal. You need to deploy a batch-processing web app whose worker capacity and plan scaling can change without changing the portal capacity. The apps must not share worker instances. Which deployment meets these requirements?

options.text: Create another Standard plan and deploy the batch app to that plan.
options.explanation: Separate plans allocate separate workers and let you change batch-plan capacity independently of the portal plan.

options.text: Deploy the batch app as a staging slot of the portal in the existing plan.
options.explanation: The slot shares its plan workers with the portal, so it does not establish the required independent capacity boundary.

options.text: Create the batch app in another resource group but select the existing plan.
options.explanation: A different resource group does not change the workers allocated by the selected plan; the apps still share compute.

options.text: Scale out the existing plan and create the batch app in that plan.
options.explanation: More instances enlarge the shared pool; they do not create a separate worker pool or independent plan scaling for the batch app.

questions.prompt: After the last web app is deleted, an administrator explicitly retains its pay-as-you-go Standard App Service plan. The empty plan still has two allocated instances and continues to accrue compute charges. No workloads or plan configuration need to be retained. Which action stops future compute charges for this plan?

options.text: Delete the empty App Service plan.
options.explanation: The retained paid plan continues reserving workers. Deleting the unused plan releases that allocation and ends its future compute charges.

options.text: Scale the empty plan in to one instance.
options.explanation: One allocated Standard instance still incurs compute charges, although fewer instances reduce the amount.

options.text: Change the empty plan from Standard to Basic.
options.explanation: Basic is also a paid dedicated tier; a lower tier does not end charges for the allocated plan.

options.text: Disable autoscale while leaving two instances allocated.
options.explanation: Disabling autoscale does not release the two allocated workers; billing follows their allocation, not whether scaling rules are enabled.

questions.prompt: An App Service app needs more memory per worker and a higher-tier feature. Which operation addresses these requirements?

options.text: Scale up the App Service plan to a suitable SKU.
options.explanation: Scale up changes worker resources and tier features.

options.text: Only increase worker count with the existing SKU.
options.explanation: Scale out adds workers but does not increase memory per worker or unlock higher-tier features.

options.text: Only add a staging slot.
options.explanation: A slot consumes the existing plan capacity.

options.text: Only set a larger maximum autoscale count.
options.explanation: A count limit does not change the worker SKU.

questions.prompt: A Standard App Service plan normally runs two instances. It must run four instances from 08:00 to 18:00 every Monday through Friday, using UTC, and two at other times regardless of CPU demand. Which Azure Monitor autoscale configuration implements this recurring capacity schedule?

options.text: Use weekday 08:00 profiles fixed at four instances and weekday 18:00 profiles fixed at two instances.
options.explanation: Recurring profiles switch capacity at the specified times. Setting each profile minimum, default, and maximum to its required count fixes four during the workday and two after the evening switch, including the weekend.

options.text: Use weekday 08:00 profiles fixed at two instances and weekday 18:00 profiles fixed at four instances.
options.explanation: These profiles reverse the required capacity: two during the workday and four overnight.

options.text: Use daily 08:00 profiles fixed at four instances and daily 18:00 profiles fixed at two instances.
options.explanation: Daily recurrence also allocates four instances during weekend days, when the requirement is two.

options.text: Use weekday 08:00 profiles fixed at four instances and weekday 18:00 profiles also fixed at four instances.
options.explanation: The evening profile does not restore two instances; it retains four outside the required workday.

questions.prompt: A Premium v3 web app uses App Service automatic HTTP scaling. Five always-ready instances are serving requests, and one additional prewarmed instance is allocated as a buffer. The app also has a staging slot used for load testing. Which TWO statements are correct about cost and scaling support? Select two individual statements.

options.text: The allocated prewarmed instance is billable while it is held as a buffer.
options.explanation: Allocated prewarmed instances are billed even before they serve application requests; the scenario confirms that this buffer exists.

options.text: The staging-slot traffic is unsupported as input for this automatic scaling feature.
options.explanation: Automatic HTTP scaling does not support deployment-slot traffic, so that load test cannot be treated as supported production scaling input.

options.text: The prewarmed instance becomes billable only after it starts serving application requests.
options.explanation: Billing begins when the prewarmed instance is allocated, not when it becomes an active request-serving worker.

options.text: The staging slot has the same supported automatic HTTP scaling behavior as the production app.
options.explanation: The feature excludes deployment-slot traffic; production-app support does not extend it to the slot.

questions.prompt: A Standard web app has production and staging slots. Each has a different DbConnection connection string and a ReleaseLabel app setting. After a completed swap, DbConnection must remain with its environment, while ReleaseLabel must follow the deployed release. Neither setting has a special platform exception. Which deployment slot setting flags meet both requirements?

options.text: DbConnection: enabled; ReleaseLabel: disabled.
options.explanation: Slot-specific connection strings stay with the environment after the swap; the unmarked ordinary app setting follows the release configuration.

options.text: DbConnection: disabled; ReleaseLabel: disabled.
options.explanation: Both are swappable, so the environment-specific connection strings would follow the release rather than remain with their slots.

options.text: DbConnection: enabled; ReleaseLabel: enabled.
options.explanation: Both stay with their slots, so the release label would not follow the deployed release.

options.text: DbConnection: disabled; ReleaseLabel: enabled.
options.explanation: This reverses the requirements: the connection string moves and the release label remains attached to its slot.

questions.prompt: Which App Service configuration remains with its slot during a swap?

options.text: Managed identity
options.explanation: Managed identities are listed among settings that do not swap.

options.text: All application content
options.explanation: Content is the main item moved between slots.

options.text: Every ordinary unmarked app setting
options.explanation: App settings can swap unless configured sticky or subject to documented exceptions.

options.text: All runtime framework settings
options.explanation: Framework settings are among the swappable configuration items.

questions.prompt: Version 2 is swapped from staging into production, leaving version 1 in staging. Version 2 then changes an external database from schema 1 to schema 2. No later deployment occurs, and neither app version changes the database during startup or a swap. You swap the same slots back without running a database recovery operation. Which production state results?

options.text: Application version 1; external database schema 2.
options.explanation: Swapping back restores the earlier app release from staging, but does not undo the separate database mutation. Compatibility or database recovery needs its own plan.

options.text: Application version 1; external database schema 1.
options.explanation: The earlier app release returns, but the external database schema does not revert merely because the slots are swapped.

options.text: Application version 2; external database schema 1.
options.explanation: The swap returns version 1 to production and has no operation that restores schema 1.

options.text: Application version 2; external database schema 2.
options.explanation: The database remains at schema 2, but swapping the same slots back returns version 1 to the production endpoint.

questions.prompt: A Standard App Service app has www.example.com mapped with verified DNS. A valid private certificate covering that hostname is uploaded. A browser connects directly to App Service using that hostname but does not receive the uploaded certificate. Which configuration associates this hostname with that certificate?

options.text: Add an SNI TLS binding for www.example.com using the uploaded certificate.
options.explanation: The hostname-to-certificate binding selects the certificate for the custom HTTPS endpoint; uploading it alone does not establish that association.

options.text: Enable HTTPS Only without adding a certificate binding.
options.explanation: HTTPS Only redirects HTTP to HTTPS; it does not select the uploaded certificate for the custom hostname.

options.text: Set the app minimum TLS version to 1.2 without adding a binding.
options.explanation: A protocol minimum limits permitted TLS versions, not which certificate is associated with the hostname.

options.text: Add a binding for api.example.com using the uploaded certificate.
options.explanation: A binding for a different hostname does not associate the certificate with the requested www.example.com endpoint.

questions.prompt: A Standard App Service app must secure mapped first-level subdomains with a certificate covering *.example.com. Clients require a publicly trusted certificate. Which certificate acquisition and binding approach meets the wildcard requirement?

options.text: Upload a trusted wildcard private certificate as a compliant PFX, then bind it to the mapped hostnames.
options.explanation: A private certificate that includes the private key, required chain, and wildcard coverage can secure the mapped first-level subdomains through TLS bindings.

options.text: Create a free App Service managed wildcard certificate, then bind it to the mapped hostnames.
options.explanation: Free App Service managed certificates do not support wildcard names; this requested certificate cannot be issued through that option.

options.text: Reuse the platform certificate for the default azurewebsites.net hostname on the mapped hostnames.
options.explanation: The platform default-hostname certificate does not cover the custom example.com subdomains.

options.text: Upload only the wildcard public certificate without its private key, then use it for the hostname bindings.
options.explanation: A public certificate upload is for use in application code, not securing custom domains. Server-side TLS requires a compliant private certificate.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of an SNI TLS binding in App Service?

options.text: Select the hostname certificate from the server name sent during the TLS handshake, allowing a shared IP.
options.explanation: SNI conveys the requested server name during TLS so multiple hostname certificates can be served on the same IP.

options.text: Select the hostname certificate from a dedicated destination IP without requiring a server name.
options.explanation: That describes IP-based TLS selection; SNI permits hostname selection on a shared IP.

options.text: Select the hostname certificate from the URL path sent after the TLS handshake.
options.explanation: The TLS certificate must be selected during the handshake, before the encrypted HTTP request supplies its path.

options.text: Select the hostname certificate from the client source IP during the TLS handshake.
options.explanation: SNI identifies the requested server hostname, not the client source address.

questions.prompt: Which Container Apps change creates a new revision?

options.text: Changing the container image in the app template
options.explanation: Container image configuration is revision-scoped.

options.text: Changing only an existing secret value
options.explanation: Secret values are application-scoped; revisions may need restarting to consume changes.

options.text: Changing only ingress traffic weights
options.explanation: Traffic configuration is application-scoped.

options.text: Adding only a managed identity
options.explanation: Changing the identity does not itself create a new revision.

questions.prompt: A Container App has healthy revisions old and new. A canary must keep both versions active while sending 10% of HTTP ingress requests to new and the remaining traffic to old. Which complete configuration meets this requirement?

options.text: Multiple revision mode; old weight 90, new weight 10.
options.explanation: Multiple mode permits both revisions to remain active, and these weights implement the required split.

options.text: Single revision mode; old weight 90, new weight 10.
options.explanation: Single mode does not maintain the two active versions required for steady canary traffic splitting.

options.text: Multiple revision mode; old weight 10, new weight 90.
options.explanation: Both versions can be active, but this sends 90% rather than 10% to new.

options.text: Multiple revision mode; old weight 100, new weight 0.
options.explanation: Both versions can be active, but the new revision receives none of the required canary traffic.

questions.prompt: A Container App has one healthy active revision receiving 100% of traffic. External HTTP ingress is enabled, and clients reach its HTTPS endpoint. The process listens on 0.0.0.0:8080, but ingress targetPort is 80 and requests fail to reach the process. Which configuration change addresses this mismatch?

options.text: Set ingress targetPort to 8080.
options.explanation: Ingress must forward requests to the port where the process listens; the current target 80 is incorrect.

options.text: Set ingress allowInsecure to true while retaining targetPort 80.
options.explanation: This permits HTTP in addition to HTTPS; it does not fix forwarding to the wrong container port.

options.text: Increase maximum replicas while retaining targetPort 80.
options.explanation: Additional replicas with the same port mismatch still receive forwarding to the wrong port.

options.text: Reapply a traffic weight of 100 to the active revision while retaining targetPort 80.
options.explanation: The revision already receives all traffic. Reapplying the weight does not change the incorrect target port.

questions.prompt: Two Linux containers share one ACI container group. The app listens on port 8080; a helper listens on port 8081. Only port 8080 is exposed on the group public IP. Which endpoint lets the app call the helper using their shared local network?

options.text: localhost:8081
options.explanation: Containers in one group share the local network; port 8081 identifies the helper listener.

options.text: The group public IP on port 8081
options.explanation: Port 8081 is not exposed on the public endpoint. The internal helper can instead be reached through localhost.

options.text: localhost:8080
options.explanation: The local network is appropriate, but port 8080 is the app listener rather than the helper.

options.text: The image registry hostname on port 8081
options.explanation: The registry stores container images; it does not address the running helper.

questions.prompt: An ACI batch process returns exit code 0 on success and a nonzero code on failure. The configuration must explicitly request retry after failure and leave successful completion terminated. Which configuration expresses this policy while preserving the process outcome?

options.text: Restart policy OnFailure; pass through the process exit code unchanged.
options.explanation: OnFailure requests retries for nonzero exits and leaves exit-code-0 completion terminated.

options.text: Restart policy Always; pass through the process exit code unchanged.
options.explanation: Always also restarts successful termination, contrary to the requirement.

options.text: Restart policy Never; pass through the process exit code unchanged.
options.explanation: Never does not explicitly request failure retries. Documentation warns that platform restarts after nonzero exits can still occur; that caveat is not an explicit retry policy.

options.text: Restart policy OnFailure; wrap the command to return exit code 0 after every run.
options.explanation: Mapping failures to zero hides the failure outcome from OnFailure, so the policy does not receive the nonzero exit needed for a retry.

questions.prompt: A Linux ACI batch task writes result files through a mounted directory. The files must survive deletion of its container group. Which storage configuration meets the requirement?

options.text: Mount an Azure Files share for the results and retain the share after deleting the group.
options.explanation: The external share persists independently of the container group, preserving files written to the mount.

options.text: Write the results only to the container writable layer.
options.explanation: The local writable layer is not durable across deletion of the container group.

options.text: Mount an emptyDir volume for the results and delete the group after completion.
options.explanation: emptyDir can share files within the group, but its contents do not survive group deletion.

options.text: Mount an Azure Files share for the results and delete that share with the group.
options.explanation: The storage is external, but deleting the share removes the retained results the requirement needs.

questions.prompt: An ACR registry uses RBAC Registry + ABAC Repository Permissions. A workload with only AcrPull cannot pull the known repository apps/web. Connectivity and authentication succeed. It must read that repository without permission to push, delete, or list every repository. Which role configuration addresses the authorization gap?

options.text: Container Registry Repository Reader with a condition covering apps/web.
options.explanation: Repository Reader grants image read/pull in ABAC mode, and the condition limits repository access without adding catalog-listing or write permissions.

options.text: AcrPull reassigned at the registry scope.
options.explanation: Legacy AcrPull is not honored in this registry mode; reassigning it does not grant repository pull access.

options.text: Container Registry Repository Catalog Lister only.
options.explanation: Catalog listing exposes repository names; it does not grant image pull and exceeds the stated listing requirement.

options.text: Reader on the registry resource only.
options.explanation: Control-plane Reader does not authorize repository image access in this mode.

questions.prompt: A deployment must refer to the exact same container image content after a tag is reassigned. Which identifier should it record?

options.text: The image digest
options.explanation: A digest identifies content rather than a mutable tag label.

options.text: Only the latest tag
options.explanation: latest is a mutable tag and may refer to different content later.

options.text: Only the repository name
options.explanation: A repository can contain many image versions.

options.text: Only the registry resource group
options.explanation: A management container does not identify image content.

questions.prompt: An App Service app must pull a private image from an ACR registry using RBAC Registry Permissions mode. The app has a system-assigned managed identity and network access to the registry, which accepts ARM-audience tokens. It must pull without storing a registry password or granting push permission. Which configuration meets the requirements?

options.text: Configure managed-identity image pulls and grant the app identity AcrPull on the registry.
options.explanation: App Service supports managed-identity pulls. AcrPull authorizes read/pull in the stated registry mode without granting push.

options.text: Configure managed-identity image pulls and grant the app identity Reader on the registry.
options.explanation: Control-plane Reader does not supply the image pull permission needed by the app.

options.text: Configure registry admin credentials as the app image-pull credentials.
options.explanation: The admin account uses a shared registry password, which the requirement excludes.

questions.prompt: You need Azure Backup historical reports across several vaults. Which data path is documented for the reporting workbooks?

options.text: Vault diagnostics sent to Log Analytics workspaces.
options.explanation: Azure Backup reporting uses Azure Monitor Logs and workbooks over exported vault diagnostic data.

options.text: Only VM guest Heartbeat records collected by Azure Monitor Agent.

options.text: Only NSG effective security rules.

questions.prompt: You enabled vault diagnostics an hour ago. A completed backup from the current day is not yet visible in Backup Reports. What should you check before treating this as a reporting failure?

options.text: Whether the backup retention policy is set to one hour.

options.text: Whether deleting the vault forces immediate report refresh.

options.text: Initial diagnostic-delivery delay, completed-day reporting, and the selected filters.

questions.prompt: Your backups retain recovery points for one year, but reporting logs are retained for only a month. You need historical backup reporting over a longer period. What should you change?

options.text: Only the backup recovery-point retention policy.
options.explanation: Backup retention does not extend the lifetime of diagnostic records in Log Analytics.

options.text: The relevant Log Analytics data retention, considering reporting requirements and cost.

options.text: Only the target VM's disk SKU.

options.text: Only the action group's email recipient.

questions.prompt: A backed-up Azure VM has been deleted. You want to recover it from a valid point. Which mode fits this situation?

options.text: Create new VM, or restore disks and construct a VM.
options.explanation: These modes do not require the original VM resource to exist.

options.text: Replace existing disks on the deleted VM.

options.text: Only change the backup schedule.

options.text: Only acknowledge its alert.
options.explanation: Alert response state does not restore the VM.

questions.prompt: A recovery point is crash-consistent. What should you expect during recovery?

options.text: Every in-memory write is guaranteed present.
options.explanation: Crash consistency captures on-disk state, not all pending memory writes.

options.text: Application/OS recovery may be needed for the captured disk state.
options.explanation: Crash-consistent recovery can require checks or transaction recovery.

options.text: The point cannot contain any disk data.
options.explanation: It does capture disk state.

options.text: It is automatically a database transaction-log backup.

questions.prompt: Azure reports a VM restore job completed. Which two checks establish practical recovery better than the job state alone?

options.text: Verify the restored VM boots with its intended disks/network.
options.explanation: Infrastructure usability needs a direct check.

options.text: Assume every external DNS entry changed automatically.
options.explanation: External references may need independent repair.

options.text: Verify guest data and application behavior at the restored point.
options.explanation: Business recovery requires more than resource creation.

options.text: Delete the recovery points immediately before checking the app.
options.explanation: That removes fallback without establishing usability.

questions.prompt: A VM and subnet appear connected in Network Insights topology. What does this establish?

options.text: Their represented resource relationship.
options.explanation: Topology does not by itself prove application-level reachability.

options.text: Every TCP port on the VM is reachable.
options.explanation: Listeners and filtering must be tested separately.

options.text: The VM's guest login succeeds.
options.explanation: Topology does not validate guest credentials.

options.text: Continuous probes have automatically been configured.
options.explanation: Inventory visibility does not create those tests.

questions.prompt: Network Insights shows a source Azure VM and destination endpoint, but no connection tests are configured. You need recurring measurements of their TCP reachability and round-trip time, with history across the day. Which Network Watcher capability supplies that monitoring?

options.text: Run one Connection troubleshoot diagnostic for the endpoint.
options.explanation: A single diagnostic examines current connectivity; it does not configure recurring monitoring history.

options.text: Configure a Connection Monitor test for the source, destination, and TCP port.
options.explanation: Connection Monitor repeatedly tests the configured endpoints and records reachability and round-trip measurements.

options.text: Run Next hop for the destination IP.

options.text: Run IP flow verify for the source VM and destination port.
options.explanation: Filtering-rule evaluation does not configure recurring live connection and latency tests.

questions.prompt: You need a new supported Network Watcher flow-logging configuration for traffic across a VNet, with IP addresses and ports recorded in Storage. The VNet has several VM subnets. options.text: Create new NSG flow logs for every subnet NSG.

options.text: Configure Connection Monitor synthetic tests between selected VM pairs.
options.explanation: Synthetic reachability tests do not record the VNet’s observed traffic flows into Storage.

options.text: Configure virtual network flow logs for the VNet and its Storage destination.
options.explanation: VNet flow logs record supported observed IP traffic at VNet scope and are the current replacement for NSG flow logs.

options.text: Run a packet capture on one VM in one subnet.
options.explanation: A per-VM capture does not provide the requested VNet-scoped flow-logging configuration across several subnets.

questions.prompt: You change Storage Insights' availability color threshold in a copied workbook. What changes?

options.explanation: Workbook formatting does not change service availability or create a rule.

options.text: The account's replication mode.
options.explanation: The workbook setting does not configure redundancy.

questions.prompt: A Standard storage account in West Europe must archive its Blob resource logs using a diagnostic setting. Candidate destination accounts already exist and the required access and firewall settings are configured. Which storage destination is supported?

questions.prompt: Which collection path supplies the Azure Storage platform metrics used by Storage Insights, including capacity and service transactions?

options.text: Performance counters collected from client VMs through an AMA DCR.

options.text: Syslog messages collected from client VMs into a Log Analytics workspace.
options.explanation: Client Syslog is guest event data, not the platform storage capacity or transaction metrics.

options.text: Azure’s automatic collection of storage service platform metrics.
options.explanation: Storage Insights uses storage metrics collected by Azure by default; a client VM agent is not required.

options.text: Parsing archived Blob resource-operation logs as the prerequisite for the built-in metric views.
options.explanation: Resource-log export is a separate configured path; it is not required to populate default Storage Insights platform metrics.

questions.prompt: An Azure VM has host CPU metrics but enhanced guest monitoring is not enabled. You need guest memory performance data in the classic logs-based monitoring experience. Required permissions and destination access are available. Which collection configuration meets the goal?

options.text: Enable logs-based enhanced monitoring with AMA, the required performance DCR association, and a Log Analytics workspace.
options.explanation: Guest counters require collection inside the VM; the classic experience uses its performance collection configuration and Log Analytics destination.

options.text: Associate an AMA DCR selecting only Windows event logs and the Log Analytics destination.
options.explanation: Guest event-log collection alone does not select the required guest memory performance counters.

options.text: Associate an AMA DCR selecting only Linux Syslog and the Log Analytics destination.
options.explanation: Syslog messages are a different data source from the required memory performance measurements.

options.text: Export only VM platform metrics through a diagnostic setting to the Log Analytics workspace.
options.explanation: Exporting host metrics does not enable collection of the missing guest memory data.

questions.prompt: A new VM deployment needs supported guest performance monitoring, without a requirement for the legacy dependency Map. An old guide includes Dependency Agent and VM Insights Map in every deployment. Which plan follows Microsoft’s current guidance?

options.text: Install Dependency Agent alone and use it for guest performance collection.
options.explanation: Dependency Agent is not the supported AMA guest performance collection path; the deprecated Map feature should not be enabled for new deployments.

options.text: Configure AMA and supported guest performance collection, and omit the deprecated Map/Dependency Agent feature.

options.text: Configure AMA guest performance collection and also enable Map/Dependency Agent for every new VM.
options.explanation: The additional legacy feature conflicts with the explicit guidance not to enable it for new deployments.

options.text: Use only the legacy Log Analytics agent for the new guest monitoring deployment.
options.explanation: The legacy agent is no longer supported; current guidance uses Azure Monitor Agent.

questions.prompt: You configure the supported OpenTelemetry guest-metrics experience for an Azure VM, rather than classic logs-based metrics. Which resource type stores those collected metrics?

options.text: A Log Analytics workspace.
options.explanation: This is the destination for classic logs-based VM monitoring and guest logs, not this OpenTelemetry metrics experience.

options.text: An Event Hubs namespace.
options.explanation: An event-streaming namespace is not the destination specified by the VM OpenTelemetry metrics workflow.

options.text: An Azure Monitor workspace.

options.text: A Storage account.
options.explanation: Archive storage is not the metrics destination for the specified enhanced monitoring workflow.

questions.prompt: Azure Monitor Agent is healthy on vm-linux and its identity and ingestion connectivity are verified. dcr-syslog defines the required Linux facilities, severity levels, and workspace destination, but its associations list contains only vm-other. Which change applies this existing collection configuration to vm-linux?

options.text: Create a DCR association between vm-linux and dcr-syslog.
options.explanation: The association makes the existing source and destination configuration apply to this VM.

options.text: Move vm-linux into the resource group containing dcr-syslog without adding an association.
options.explanation: Resource-group membership does not associate the DCR with the VM.

options.text: Create another copy of dcr-syslog without associating that copy with vm-linux.
options.explanation: A second unassociated rule still does not apply its collection configuration to this VM.

options.text: Change the destination of dcr-syslog to another workspace without changing associations.
options.explanation: The VM remains unassociated regardless of the selected destination.

questions.prompt: A Windows VM sends current Heartbeat records to ws-ops through Azure Monitor Agent. A locally generated Security event in the test window is missing from the correctly scoped Event-table query in ws-ops. Its associated DCR currently selects only System events. No other event collector is configured. Which change addresses the observed missing stream?

options.text: Reinstall the healthy agent while retaining the System-only DCR.
options.explanation: The supplied filter still excludes Security events; reinstalling the agent does not select that stream.

options.text: Add a Windows Security-event selection that includes the test event to the DCR’s ws-ops data flow.
options.explanation: Heartbeat establishes communication, but the DCR must separately select the required event source and route it to the workspace.

options.text: Increase workspace retention while retaining the System-only DCR.
options.explanation: Retention controls stored data lifetime, not selection of an uncollected event stream.

options.text: Extend the query time window while retaining the System-only DCR.
options.explanation: The query already covers the known event time. A broader search does not collect events excluded by the DCR.

questions.prompt: For Azure Monitor Agent collection from VMs, which statement correctly distinguishes a DCR from its associations?

options.text: The DCR lists linked VMs; each association defines a separate set of event filters.
options.explanation: The relationship is reversed: source filters belong to the DCR and associations link resources to it.

options.text: The DCR installs the guest operating system; associations install application packages.
options.explanation: DCRs and associations configure telemetry collection rather than guest OS or application deployment.

options.text: The DCR defines collection sources and destinations; associations apply it to selected VMs.
options.explanation: The rule describes collection and routing, and the VM-to-rule association applies that configuration.

options.text: The DCR defines resource retention; associations contain the stored event records.
options.explanation: Collection rules and resource links are not the stored event data or workspace retention configuration.

questions.prompt: A resource exposes a supported audit log category and has platform metrics visible. You need its future audit operations in workspace ws-audit. Both ws-audit and ws-metrics exist and you have the required configuration access. Which diagnostic setting collects the requested data at the required destination?

options.text: Enable the resource audit log category; destination ws-audit.
options.explanation: Resource logs require collection of the relevant category and export to the intended workspace.

options.text: Enable only AllMetrics; destination ws-audit.
options.explanation: This exports numeric platform metrics rather than the required resource audit log records.

options.text: Enable the resource audit log category; destination ws-metrics.
options.explanation: The data category is correct, but the logs are sent to the wrong workspace.

options.text: Export only the subscription Activity Log; destination ws-audit.
options.explanation: Management events are a different source from the specified resource audit operations.

questions.prompt: A resource must export the same supported audit category to existing workspaces ws-operations and ws-security. No diagnostic settings exist and required access is available. Use direct diagnostic-settings export. Which design sends each future audit event to both workspaces?

options.text: One setting containing both workspaces as Log Analytics destinations.
options.explanation: One setting can contain only one destination of each type, including a single Log Analytics workspace.

options.text: Two settings enabling the audit category, each targeting one of the workspaces.
options.explanation: Separate settings allow destinations of the same type; both collect the required category.

options.text: One setting targeting ws-operations, then edit that same setting to target ws-security.
options.explanation: Replacing the destination does not preserve simultaneous export to ws-operations.

options.text: Two settings: audit logs to ws-operations, and only AllMetrics to ws-security.
options.explanation: The second workspace receives metrics rather than the required copy of each audit event.

questions.prompt: You need Linux guest Syslog messages from supported Azure VMs in a Log Analytics workspace. Azure Monitor Agent is installed and its destination connectivity works. Select facilities and severity levels and collect future guest messages for queries. Which configuration supplies that collection path?

options.text: A VM resource diagnostic setting exporting only AllMetrics to the workspace.
options.explanation: AllMetrics exports platform measurements; it does not select guest Syslog facilities or severities.

options.text: A subscription diagnostic setting exporting only Activity Log events to the workspace.
options.explanation: Activity Log export collects management events, not guest Syslog messages.

options.text: A DCR with a Linux Syslog source and workspace destination, associated with the VMs.
options.explanation: The DCR selects Syslog facilities and levels and applies collection to the associated agent-equipped VMs.

options.text: A guest Syslog daemon configuration writing the selected messages only to a local file.
options.explanation: Local logging alone does not deliver messages to the required workspace.

questions.prompt: What does `Syslog | summarize Messages=count() by Computer` return?

options.text: One row per observed Computer value with its message count.
options.explanation: summarize groups the input by Computer and counts rows.

options.text: Every Syslog row with no aggregation.
options.explanation: summarize reduces rows into groups.

options.text: Only the most recent message per computer.
options.explanation: count() is not a latest-row selection.

options.text: A count of computers per message text.
options.explanation: The grouping key is Computer, not message text.

questions.prompt: A Syslog table has more than ten rows with distinct TimeGenerated timestamps in the query scope. Which query selects the ten newest messages by TimeGenerated?

options.text: Syslog | take 10
options.explanation: take limits rows without guaranteeing newest-first selection.

options.text: Syslog | top 10 by TimeGenerated desc
options.explanation: top with descending timestamp selects the ten largest timestamps, which are the newest messages.

options.text: Syslog | top 10 by TimeGenerated asc
options.explanation: Ascending timestamp selects the ten oldest messages in scope.

options.text: Syslog | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *)
options.explanation: With no grouping this produces one latest row, not the required ten messages.

questions.prompt: A known Syslog event generated two minutes ago has been verified in workspace ws-prod. You have query access, and its Computer and TimeGenerated values match your filters. The same query returns no rows when Logs is opened with workspace scope ws-test, which does not store this event. You need to retrieve the already ingested event. Which change addresses the observed scope mismatch?

options.text: Run the query with workspace scope ws-prod.
options.explanation: Workspace scope determines which stored workspace data the query searches. The verified event is in ws-prod.

options.text: Extend the time range to one day while keeping scope ws-test.
options.explanation: The event already matches the current time filter; widening time does not search the different workspace.

options.text: Reinstall the VM agent while keeping query scope ws-test.
options.explanation: The event is already ingested into ws-prod. Reinstallation does not move that stored event into the queried workspace.

options.text: Remove the Computer filter while keeping scope ws-test.
options.explanation: Removing a matching filter does not expose a record stored in ws-prod to a ws-test-scoped query.

questions.prompt: A CPU-percentage metric supports Average and Maximum at one-minute granularity. A chart averages each 30-minute interval, masking short spikes. You must inspect the highest collected value in each minute of the incident window. Which chart configuration meets the goal?

options.text: Maximum aggregation; one-minute time grain.
options.explanation: Each point reports the highest collected value in its one-minute interval.

options.text: Average aggregation; one-minute time grain.
options.explanation: Finer intervals help localize changes, but averaging does not preserve the highest sample in each interval.

options.text: Maximum aggregation; 30-minute time grain.
options.explanation: It exposes a peak for each 30-minute interval rather than the required per-minute peaks.

options.text: Average aggregation; 30-minute time grain with a shorter displayed time range.
options.explanation: A shorter displayed range does not change the explicitly retained aggregation or interval size.

questions.prompt: An application metric exposes an Instance dimension with four worker values. All four workers have data in the selected window. You need four separate worker series on one Metrics explorer chart, without excluding any worker. Which configuration meets the goal?

options.text: Filter Instance to one worker without applying splitting.
options.explanation: This excludes three workers and does not display all four separate series.

options.text: Split by Instance and set the displayed-series limit to at least four.
options.explanation: Splitting creates one series per dimension value; the limit must include all four workers.

options.text: Filter Instance to all four workers without applying splitting.
options.explanation: The filter includes the workers but leaves their values combined into one series.

options.text: Split by Instance and set the displayed-series limit to one.
options.explanation: Splitting is appropriate, but the one-series limit omits three required workers.

questions.prompt: A metric records three values: 4, 6, and 10 in one interval. Which statement is correct when Count and Sum are supported?

options.text: Count and Sum both equal 20.
options.explanation: Count measures the three samples.

options.text: Count equals the highest value, 10.
options.explanation: That is Maximum, not Count.

options.text: Count is 3 and Sum is 20.
options.explanation: Samples and total measured values are different quantities.

options.text: Average is 20.
options.explanation: Average divides the sum by the sample count.

questions.prompt: An Azure VM has the required monitoring extension. You need a week of recurring TCP reachability and latency measurements to service.example on port 443. Which Connection Monitor configuration meets the goal?

options.explanation: The group associates the endpoints with recurring tests of the required protocol and port; monitoring data supplies history.

options.text: Add the VM source and destination to a test group whose only configuration uses ICMP.

options.text: Add a TCP 443 configuration to a test group that has no source endpoint.
options.explanation: A test requires a source, destination, and configuration; the source is missing.

options.text: Add the correct endpoints and TCP 443 configuration, then disable the test group for the week.
options.explanation: Disabling the group stops its tests, so it cannot collect the required recurring measurements.

questions.prompt: What combines sources, destinations, and test configurations within Connection Monitor?

options.text: An endpoint.
options.explanation: An endpoint represents a participating source or destination, rather than the container combining endpoints and configurations.

options.text: A test group.
options.explanation: A test group contains sources, destinations, and test configurations within a connection monitor.

options.text: A test configuration.
options.explanation: The configuration defines protocol-specific settings such as port and frequency; it does not contain the source and destination membership.

options.text: An individual test.
options.explanation: An individual test is one source-destination-configuration combination, rather than the group containing their collections.

questions.prompt: A Connection Monitor ICMP test from vm-app to service.example succeeds. The application uses TCP 443. You need recurring evidence that a TCP connection to that port can be established, before investigating HTTP responses. Which test configuration should you add for the same endpoints?

options.text: ICMP with a shorter test interval.
options.explanation: More frequent ICMP checks still do not test whether a TCP connection to port 443 can be established.

options.text: TCP with destination port 80.
options.explanation: Port 80 is a different listener and does not establish reachability of the required port 443.

options.text: TCP with destination port 443.
options.explanation: This tests TCP reachability to the specified application port; it does not by itself establish HTTP response correctness.

options.text: TCP with destination port 22.
options.explanation: An SSH-port check targets a different listener and cannot establish the required TCP 443 reachability.

questions.prompt: A VNet flow-log record shows source and destination IPs, ports, protocol, and byte counts for a TCP 443 flow. Which evidence can you obtain from that record alone?

options.text: The recorded endpoints and traffic volume for the flow.
options.explanation: These are flow metadata fields; they describe the connection and recorded volume without storing its application payload.

options.text: The full HTTPS request body sent over the flow.
options.explanation: A byte count measures volume and does not contain the application body.

options.text: The HTTP response status returned by the application.
options.explanation: Flow metadata does not record the application-layer HTTP response status.

options.text: The user identity accepted by the application during login.
options.explanation: IP-flow metadata does not record application authentication decisions or the authenticated user.

questions.prompt: VNet flow logging is enabled with a supported Standard general-purpose v2 Storage destination. Retention is set to 0 days, and no other deletion policy applies. What happens to stored flow-log data?

options.text: Delete each log immediately.
options.explanation: Zero is not immediate expiry in this setting.

options.text: Retain indefinitely until manually removed.
options.explanation: This is the documented meaning of zero.

options.text: Disable flow collection.

options.text: Keep only denied flows.
options.explanation: Retention does not select the flow action.

questions.prompt: New VNet flow-log blobs are arriving in Storage. The saved configuration has traffic analytics disabled. You need processed traffic data in ws-network without changing raw log collection. Which change meets the goal?

options.text: Keep analytics disabled and set raw-log retention to 30 days.
options.explanation: Retention changes how long raw blobs remain; it does not enable their processing into the workspace.

options.text: Keep analytics disabled and change the raw-log Storage account.
options.explanation: Changing the raw destination does not enable processing into Log Analytics.

options.text: Enable traffic analytics, select ws-network, and set its processing interval.
options.explanation: This configures the separate analytics stage for the arriving flow data and sends processed data to the intended workspace.

options.text: Enable traffic analytics with ws-other as its workspace.
options.explanation: Analytics would target a different workspace and would not meet the required ws-network destination.

questions.prompt: A VM now runs in the secondary region after a committed Site Recovery failover. You choose Re-Protect to prepare for returning to the primary. What does this do?

options.text: Immediately moves production execution to the primary.
options.explanation: Reprotection starts reverse replication; failback is a later recovery operation.

options.text: Deletes all backups in a Backup vault.
options.explanation: Site Recovery reprotection is not an Azure Backup deletion operation.

options.text: Keeps only primary-to-secondary replication without collecting secondary changes.
options.explanation: Returning safely requires replication of changes from the current secondary VM toward the primary.

options.text: Replicates from the secondary region toward the primary region.
options.explanation: This is the documented reverse replication direction after failover.

questions.prompt: A VM was failed over and reprotected from secondary to primary using Site Recovery. Before failback, which two checks are required by the tutorial?

options.text: The replicated VM is healthy/protected and synchronization is complete.
options.explanation: Failback should use a healthy, synchronized replicated item.

options.text: The original primary VM is powered on to receive disk changes.
options.explanation: The tutorial requires the original primary-region VM to be shut down; an active VM can make failback fail.

options.text: The primary region is available and required resource access is permitted.
options.explanation: Availability and resource permissions are prerequisites for returning to that region.

options.text: All replication recovery points are deleted before the failback starts.
options.explanation: Failback uses a selected recovery point; deleting them beforehand is not a prerequisite.

questions.prompt: A Site Recovery failback has returned your VM to the primary region. What restores disaster recovery coverage toward the secondary region?

options.text: Assume protection has resumed without checking replication.
options.explanation: The tutorial calls for reprotection after failback.

options.text: Reprotect the primary VM toward the secondary and verify replication health.
options.explanation: This restores the intended primary-to-secondary replication direction.

options.text: Leave reverse replication permanently configured toward the primary.
options.explanation: Once execution is primary again, the intended recovery destination is the secondary.

options.text: Run Cleanup test failover instead of reprotection.
options.explanation: Test-drill cleanup is a separate workflow and does not establish production replication.

questions.prompt: During Site Recovery failover, your priority is to avoid extra processing of received replication data before recovery. Which recovery-point option fits?

options.text: Latest processed.
options.explanation: It uses an already processed point, avoiding additional recovery-point processing before failover.

options.text: Latest.
options.explanation: Latest processes received data first, favoring a more recent point rather than avoiding that processing.

options.text: Any old application-consistent point necessarily minimizes recovery time.
options.explanation: Application consistency describes recovered data consistency, not a guarantee of minimum processing/recovery time.

options.text: A backup-policy retention change.
options.explanation: A backup retention change does not choose a Site Recovery failover point.

questions.prompt: A recovered Site Recovery VM is running, but you might need a different recovery point. Which action removes the ability to change the recovery point?

options.text: Viewing the target VM's size.
options.explanation: Inspecting VM configuration does not commit failover.

options.text: Checking the failover job status.
options.explanation: Monitoring the job does not delete the available recovery points.

options.text: Committing the failover.
options.explanation: Commit deletes the available recovery points for the VM and ends recovery-point changes.

options.text: Opening the replicated item's overview.
options.explanation: Opening the overview is a read operation.

questions.prompt: You select Shut down machine before beginning failover in Site Recovery, but the source VM cannot be shut down. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Site Recovery always cancels failover automatically.
options.explanation: The tutorial states that failover continues even when source shutdown fails.

options.text: Failover can continue, so your runbook must address a potentially active source application.
options.explanation: The setting attempts shutdown; it does not guarantee shutdown or exclusive application activity.

options.text: The setting guarantees that no source writes can be lost.
options.explanation: A failed shutdown and replication state prevent such an unconditional guarantee.

options.text: The source VM is automatically converted into an offline backup.
options.explanation: The setting controls an attempted shutdown, not conversion to Azure Backup.

questions.prompt: You enable Azure-to-Azure Site Recovery for a VM. Where should the replication cache storage account be located?

options.text: Only in the target recovery region.
options.explanation: The documented replication path uses a cache account in the source region.

options.text: In the source VM's region.
options.explanation: VM changes pass through source-region cache storage before recovery processing in the target region.

options.text: In any third region chosen for backup reports.
options.explanation: Reporting placement does not determine Site Recovery cache placement.

options.text: On the VM's temporary disk instead of a storage account.
options.explanation: A temporary disk is not the replication cache storage account.

questions.prompt: An administrator has Site Recovery Contributor on a vault but cannot enable replication using another resource group's resources. What should you check?

options.text: The required permissions on the linked source and target resources.
options.explanation: Site Recovery validates permissions on the resources used by the operation, as well as vault access.

options.text: Whether the role grants subscription-wide Owner automatically.
options.explanation: A role assignment at the vault does not confer subscription-wide Owner.

options.text: Whether Site Recovery Reader would grant more write access.
options.explanation: Reader is for inspecting recovery state, not enabling replication.

options.text: Whether disabling storage encryption bypasses Azure RBAC.
options.explanation: Encryption settings do not eliminate authorization checks.

questions.prompt: A restrictive NSG blocks a source VM's Site Recovery replication. You need connectivity rules that tolerate service IP changes. What is Microsoft's recommended approach?

options.text: Pin the recovery service's current IP addresses permanently.
options.explanation: Hard-coded service IP addresses can change and break replication.

options.text: Allow only inbound RDP to the source VM.
options.explanation: Remote desktop access does not provide the outbound service connectivity replication needs.

options.text: Use the documented service tags and outbound HTTPS rules, and check storage firewall access.
options.explanation: Service tags support changing service addresses; storage firewall permissions still need separate review.

options.text: Configure an authenticated proxy as the mandatory replication path.
options.explanation: Authenticated proxies are unsupported for Site Recovery replication.

questions.prompt: You are planning a Site Recovery disaster recovery drill while production remains active. Which target network does Microsoft recommend for the test VMs?

options.text: The production recovery network regardless of address conflicts.
options.explanation: Microsoft recommends a non-production network for drills to protect production networking availability.

options.text: A suitable non-production network in the target region.
options.explanation: This supports testing without competing with production addresses and network components.

options.text: Only the source VM's original subnet in the source region.
options.explanation: The drill recovers the VM into the chosen target-region network.

options.text: No VNet because test failover uses only an offline disk.
options.explanation: Test failover creates a VM connected to the selected target VNet.

questions.prompt: A Site Recovery test failover is finished and its observations have been recorded. How should you end the drill and remove its test VMs?

options.text: Use Cleanup test failover and confirm Testing is complete.
options.explanation: This is the documented cleanup workflow, including saving observations and deleting test VMs.

options.text: Disable replication permanently for the source VM.
options.explanation: Ending a drill does not require removing the source VM's disaster recovery protection.

options.text: Commit a production failover.
options.explanation: A production failover commit is a different workflow from test cleanup.

options.text: Delete the Recovery Services vault immediately.
options.explanation: Deleting the vault is neither necessary nor the drill cleanup procedure.

questions.prompt: A team member should run Site Recovery drills and failover/failback operations, but must not enable or disable replication. Which recovery role fits, with required linked-resource read access supplied separately?

options.text: Site Recovery Reader.
options.explanation: Reader can inspect recovery state but cannot perform the requested operations.

options.text: Site Recovery Contributor.
options.explanation: Contributor includes replication management, exceeding the stated recovery-operation scope.

options.text: Site Recovery Operator.
options.explanation: Operator supports failover/failback operations while excluding enable/disable replication.

options.text: Storage Blob Data Reader.
options.explanation: Blob data access does not authorize Site Recovery operations.

questions.prompt: An Azure Monitor action group's sample email test fails. What can you conclude about a separate metric alert rule's threshold evaluation from this result alone?

options.text: Nothing definitive; the sample tests the action path, not the metric condition.
options.explanation: Investigate delivery separately and check real rule evaluation using its own state and telemetry.

options.text: The metric threshold is definitely false.
options.explanation: Sample delivery does not evaluate the metric threshold.

options.text: The real metric rule definitely fired.
options.explanation: Sending a sample does not establish that the real rule evaluated true.

options.text: The VM definitely stopped emitting metric samples.
options.explanation: A notification-path failure does not prove loss of metric collection.

questions.prompt: A VM has maintenance every Friday from 02:00 to 03:00 UTC. Keep metric-alert evaluation active and suppress action groups only during that recurring hour, including future Fridays. Which processing-rule schedule meets the requirement?

options.text: VM scope; suppress action groups; weekly Friday 02:00–03:00 UTC.
options.explanation: Weekly Friday recurrence covers the repeated maintenance hour without suppressing other days.

options.text: VM scope; suppress action groups; a one-time window for this Friday 02:00–03:00 UTC.
options.explanation: A one-time window does not cover later Fridays.

options.text: VM scope; suppress action groups; weekly Saturday 02:00–03:00 UTC.
options.explanation: The recurring day is wrong, so Friday maintenance is not covered.

options.text: VM scope; suppress action groups; daily 02:00–03:00 UTC.
options.explanation: Daily recurrence suppresses six additional days, contrary to the Friday-only requirement.

questions.prompt: Two VNets are peered and use Azure-provided DNS. A private zone contains a verified A record for db.corp.example and has a completed link only to vnet-a. A VM in vnet-a resolves it, but a VM in vnet-b cannot. Which change gives vnet-b access to the existing zone records?

options.text: Add a resolution-only link from the existing private zone to vnet-b.
options.explanation: The client VNet needs its own zone link with Azure-provided DNS. Autoregistration is unnecessary to resolve existing records.

options.text: Enable autoregistration on the existing link to vnet-a.
options.explanation: This registers vnet-a VM names; it does not link vnet-b to the zone.

options.text: Recreate the peering between the VNets without changing zone links.
options.explanation: Peering supplies network connectivity, not a private-zone link for vnet-b.

options.text: Create an empty second private zone and link only that zone to vnet-b.
options.explanation: An empty separate zone does not expose the verified record in the existing zone.

questions.prompt: You link a VNet to a private zone with autoregistration disabled. What does this link provide?

options.text: Automatic registration of every VM name.
options.explanation: That requires autoregistration enabled.

options.text: Resolution of records in the linked zone without automatic VM registration.
options.explanation: This is a resolution-only link.

options.text: Public Internet resolution of the zone.
options.explanation: The link serves private-network resolution.

options.text: Automatic VNet peering to all other linked networks.
options.explanation: DNS links do not create network peerings.

questions.prompt: A VNet using Azure-provided DNS has a completed link to alpha.example with autoregistration enabled. It must also resolve existing private records in beta.example while continuing to register its VM names only in alpha.example. Which final link configuration meets the requirements?

options.text: Keep alpha autoregistration enabled; add beta with autoregistration enabled.
options.explanation: A VNet can have only one registration zone. Two enabled registration links are not supported.

options.text: Disable alpha autoregistration; add beta with autoregistration disabled.
options.explanation: Both zones can resolve, but this stops the required VM-name registration in alpha.

options.text: Keep alpha autoregistration enabled; add beta with autoregistration disabled.
options.explanation: The existing registration zone remains alpha; the additional resolution-only link supplies beta lookups.

options.text: Disable alpha autoregistration; add beta with autoregistration enabled.
options.explanation: This moves registration to beta, contrary to the requirement to keep it only in alpha.

questions.prompt: You migrated example.org to an Azure public DNS zone. Queries sent directly to its assigned Azure name servers return the new www A record. A fresh delegation trace still reaches the previous provider. Which configuration should you change to direct Internet DNS resolution to the new zone?

options.text: Set the registrar delegation to all four name servers assigned to the Azure zone.
options.explanation: The parent delegation selects authoritative servers. It must reference the four servers assigned to this zone.

options.text: Replace the www A record in the previous provider with the new address.
options.explanation: This might update that provider’s answer but keeps it authoritative; the goal is to move resolution to the Azure zone.

options.text: Lower the www A record TTL in the Azure zone.
options.explanation: TTL controls caching of that answer. It does not change the parent delegation that still selects the previous provider.

options.text: Copy the previous provider’s name servers into an NS record set named www in Azure.
options.explanation: A child-name NS set does not update example.org’s registrar delegation and would point www back to the old servers.

questions.prompt: The public zone example.org must return the IPv4 address of a Standard SKU Azure public IP resource at its apex and track the resource automatically. The resource provider and required permissions are configured. Which record set meets both requirements?

options.text: An apex CNAME targeting the public IP resource hostname.
options.explanation: A CNAME cannot coexist with the apex SOA and NS record sets.

options.text: An apex A alias targeting the public IP resource.
options.explanation: An A alias can reference a Standard public IP resource at the apex and follow its resource lifecycle.

options.text: An apex A record containing a manually copied IPv4 address.
options.explanation: It answers with IPv4, but a literal address is not linked to the public IP resource and does not track it automatically.

options.text: An apex AAAA alias targeting the public IP resource.
options.explanation: AAAA answers are IPv6. The requested answer is IPv4, which requires an A record set.
